几何拓扑方向研究课题覆盖的方向较全面，如微分几何、几何分析、Teichmüller 理论、低维拓扑、高维流形拓扑、复几何等。 组长： 林剑锋 副组长： 高鸿灏 教授： 丘成桐、Kenji Fukaya、Akito Futaki、林勇、Vladimir Markovic、吴云辉 副教授：林剑锋、肖建、高鸿灏 助理教授：陈伟彦、孙巍峰、朱波、朱知非 博士后：Choudhury 分析、PDE、动力系统研究有限维和无限维状态空间随定律的时间演化。历史上，对这些问题的研究与数学其它学科的发展联系密切，研究中需要运用分析、拓扑、群论等方法，不少数学理论在这些问题的研究基础上发展起来。研究方向有：动力系统、相对论与波方程、流体力学、椭圆偏微分方程、拟随机群和Cayley图等。 组长：王学成 副组长：荆文甲 教授：陈志杰、 张翼华 副教授：金龙、荆文甲 、王学成 数学物理是数学和物理的交叉领域，应用特定的数学方法来研究物理学的某些部分。也利用物理学的方法计算数学中的对象。数学和物理学的发展，历史上一直密不可分，许多数学理论是在物理问题的基础上发展起来的，很多数学方法和工具通常也只在物理学中找到实际应用。主要研究方向：超弦理论，量子引力，规范/引力对偶、超对称场论及其在几何中的应用、范畴论与凝聚态物理中的拓扑序等。 组长：宋伟 副组长：周杰 教授： David、Nikolaos Angelinos、Sarthak Duary、Singh Rahul、Galviz Blanco Daniel Eduardo、陈良玉、靳安然、阮钰泽、邵钰菓、许容阁、潘俏尹、葛东胜、魏付川、赵子烁、杨培赫、冯凌璇 弦论研究团队 https://ymsc-strings.github.io/seminar.html 应用数学方向 计算和应用数学关注使用数学理论和方法来解决实际问题，以及通过数值方法对数学模型进行计算和分析。这一领域涵盖了诸如数学建模、数值分析、优化、反问题、数据科学、密码学等多个子领域，被广泛应用于工程、物理、经济、金融、生物学等多个学科。计算和应用数学不仅提供工具来近似解决复杂的数学问题，同时也为各领域的科学研究和工程实践提供了坚实的理论支撑。主要研究方向包括：后量子密码学、数学建模、数值分析、偏微分方程数值解、计算动力系统、数值代数、反问题、图像处理、大规模优化方法、材料科学的数学理论与计算、应用分析、机器学习理论、运营和收益管理理论。 统计学是数据科学的基础，也是其核心组成部分之一。它是关于数据收集、数据分析、解释及推断的理论和方法的学问，并广泛用于科学、工程、医学、金融、政府管理等等领域，获取各种数据背后的信息、规律以及对其不确定性进行可靠的勾画，并以此对未来进行相对准确的预测。主要研究方向包括：因果推断、缺失数据、模型选择和平均、多臂老虎机、高维数据和机器学习等。 组长：杨宇红 副组长：杨帆(男) 教授： Per AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: ICLR 2027 - Call for Workshops Following the ICLR 2027 main conference, two days of in-person workshops on a variety of current topics will be held on April 29 and 30, 2026 in San Francisco, California, US . We invite researchers interested in organizing a workshop to submit proposals. Workshop organizers have several responsibilities, including coordinating workshop participation and content, publicizing and providing the program in a timely manner, and moderating the program throughout the workshop. Goal of ICLR Workshops Workshops provide an informal, cutting edge venue for discussion of works in progress and future directions. Good workshops have helped to crystallize common problems, explicitly contrast competing frameworks, and clarify essential questions for a subfield or application area. Workshops are a structured means of bringing together people with common interests to form communities. Good workshops should include some form of community building. Each workshop is a single-day, in-person event, split into morning and afternoon sessions, with free time between the sessions for individual exchange. Workshop topics should include, but are not limited to, the following: unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised representation learning representation learning for planning and reinforcement learning representation learning for computer vision and natural language processing metric learning and kernel learning sparse coding and dimensionality expansion optimization for representation learning probabilistic inference and learning theoretical issues in deep learning societal considerations of representation learning including fairness, safety, privacy, and interpretability, and explainability visualization or interpretation of learned representations implementation issues, parallelization, software platforms, hardware sustainability in AI and AI for sustainability applications in natural and life sciences, audio, speech, robotics, or any other field Detailed descriptions of previous workshops may be found in last year's blog post . Workshop schedules should encourage lively debates, stimulate the production of new ideas and foster discussion of important issues. Workshop organizers are recommended to follow the Policies on Large Language Model Usage at ICLR 2027. Workshops that allow AI to serve as a primary author and/or reviewer of workshop papers should clearly state the role of AI participation in their workshop proposal. The conference will provide tools to flag AI-generated papers, reviews, and meta-reviews. To encourage diversity across workshop programs, each individual may be listed as a speaker, panelist, or in a similar invited role in no more than two distinct workshop proposals . Proposals must include the OpenReview IDs of all invited speakers, panelists, and others participating in a similar manner. These IDs will help the workshop chairs identify overlap across proposals and make sure of broader participation. Organizers should confirm that each invitee has agreed to be listed and is included in no more than two workshop proposals. If a proposal is accepted and the list of invited speakers, panelists, or other participants changes, the corresponding information must be updated on OpenReview. Please also note this year’s limits on workshop organizers. As a general rule, each proposal should include no more than eight organizers, and each organizer must disclose any other workshop proposals they are helping to organize. Each role, whether an advisory role or a student volunteer role, counts toward the limit of eight organizers. In addition, an individual may be listed as an organizer on no more than two workshop proposals. As a new requirement this year, we ask each workshop to nominate one or more mid-career or senior researchers who are not among the workshop organizers to serve on the workshop proposal review committee. This will help us accommodate the growing number of submissions and encourage workshops to contribute back to the broader ICLR workshop community. Finally, please be aware that creating a new OpenReview account may take two weeks or longer, so organizers and invited participants should register well in advance of the submission deadline. Every group considering submitting a workshop proposal should read the ICLR 2027 Workshop Proposal Guide , which outlines the relevant constraints and describes important considerations for hosting workshops, includes templates of previous successful proposals, details the selection criteria and process, describes what is considered a conflict of interest, and includes other frequently asked questions. Submission Instructions Proposals should be submitted through an application on OpenReview at: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICLR.cc/2027/Workshop_Proposals Note that all proposal organizers, speakers and panelists are required to have an OpenReview profile. Please create an OpenReview Profile at least two weeks before the workshop application deadline on 9 October 2026. Important dates for workshop organizers Workshop Application Open : 8 September 2026 Workshop Application Deadline : 9 October 2026, 11.59pm AoE Workshop Acceptance Notification : 7 December 2026 Suggested Submission Deadline for Workshop Contributions: 1 Feb 2027 Mandatory Accepted Paper Notification Date*: 26 February 2027, 11.59pm AoE * By this deadline, workshop organizers must (1) notify authors of acceptance decisions, (2) make all accepted papers publicly available on OpenReview, and (3) import all accepted papers into iclr.cc. Meeting this deadline is particularly important for workshop contributors who plan to apply for ICLR financial assistance or require a visa letter. Update Workshop Schedule with Opening and Closing Times on iclr.cc: 26 March 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE Complete and Finalize Workshop Schedules in the Organizer Portal: 14 April 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE The criteria and process by which proposals will be assessed are described in the ICLR 2027 Workshop Proposal Guide . Organizer Support The organizers of each accepted workshop can name four individuals to receive a full-conference complimentary registration. ICLR 2027 Workshop Chairs Nezihe Merve Gürel (TU Delft) Yuanqi Du (Microsoft Research) Chulin Xie (Google DeepMind) Antonio Vergari (University of Edinburgh) Contact Email : workshop-chairs@iclr.cc

items.content: ICLR 2027 Workshop Proposal Guide ICLR 2027 - Call for Workshops ICLR Workshop Co-Chairs Nezihe Merve Gürel (TU Delft) Yuanqi Du (Microsoft Research) Chulin Xie (Google DeepMind) Antonio Vergari (University of Edinburgh) This is the ninth year that ICLR will have workshops. With the rapid growth and interest in ICLR and its associated workshops, the competition for workshops has grown. To guide and support submissions, the workshop chairs have agreed on the following guidance for proposals to hold a workshop at ICLR 2027. Organizers of workshop proposals should take care to respect every piece of guidance provided here, and provide explicit answers to the questions implied throughout, as well as explicitly addressing the selection criteria listed below. Timeline Workshop Application Open : 8 September 2026 Workshop Application Deadline : 9 October 2026, 11.59pm AoE Workshop Acceptance Notification : 7 December 2026 Suggested Submission Deadline for Workshop Contributions: 1 Feb 2027 Mandatory Accepted Paper Notification Date*: 26 February 2027, 11.59pm AoE * By this deadline, workshop organizers must (1) notify authors of acceptance decisions, (2) make all accepted papers publicly available on OpenReview, and (3) import all accepted papers into iclr.cc. Meeting this deadline is particularly important for workshop contributors who plan to apply for ICLR financial assistance or require a visa letter. Update Workshop Schedule with Opening and Closing Times on iclr.cc: 26 March 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE Complete and Finalize Workshop Schedules in the Organizer Portal: 14 April 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE The mandatory author notification deadline of 26 February 2027 will not be extended. Note that all proposal organizers, speakers and panelists are required to have an OpenReview profile. Please create an OpenReview Profile at least two weeks before the workshop application deadline on 9 October 2026. Selection Criteria Degree to which the proposal is focused on an important and topical problem, and the degree to which it is expected that the community will find the workshop interesting, exciting, and valuable. Intellectual excitement of the topic. Is it likely to break new ground, or reiterate past debates? Diversity and inclusion. (See expectations below under Other Guidance and Expectations for Workshop Proposals. ) Degree to which the proposed program offers an opportunity for discussion. Degree to which the proposal creates opportunities for under-represented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to engage with the community. (See requirements below under Platform for Tiny or Short Papers .) Quality of proposed invited speakers (including expertise, scientific achievements, and presentation ability). Workshop organizers are required to confirm tentative interest from proposed invited speakers and mention this in their proposal. Degree to which the organizers have offered means to engage in the workshop for those unable to physically attend given that the workshops will be in-person. Organizational experience of the team. Other dimensions in the expectations listed below. Points of difference. What makes this workshop enticingly different to the ICLR workshops held previously? Assessment Process The workshop chairs will appoint a number of reviewers who will provide written assessments of the proposals against the criteria listed above. Reviews will be released to authors. Their reports will be considered by the workshop chairs who will jointly decide upon the selected workshops (subject to the notes on COIs listed below). The final decisions will be made by the workshop chairs via consensus and judgment. Note that in contrast to the number of papers accepted at most conferences there is a natural limit to the number of workshops that can be accepted, dictated by the number of available rooms at the conference venue. Workshop Requirements Honor the Global Notification Deadline Prior until 26 February 2027 By submitting a workshop proposal, workshop organizers commit to notifying those who submit contributions (including talks and posters) to their workshop of their acceptance status before 11.59pm, 26 February 2027 (AOE). In addition, the organizers must make the accepted papers publicly visible on OpenReview and import them into iclr.cc by this date. A timeline should be included in the proposal that will allow for this. Platform Contributed Work Ensure that contributed work is well-featured in the program, and is given visibility through presentation slots and poster sessions. Additionally, your workshop program should effectively engage the audience by allowing for interactive components. Platform for Tiny or Short Papers We encourage each workshop to establish a tiny or short paper track to encourage the submission of late-breaking developments that would most benefit from feedback at ICLR, as well to make their workshops more accessible to potential authors outside the ML conference publication circuit. This tiny or short paper track should prioritize less-than-full-conference papers, welcoming submissions that, for example, present an implementation and evaluation of an unpublished but simple idea, a modest but self-contained theoretical result, a follow-up experiment or re-analysis of a previously published paper, or a fresh perspective on an existing publication. To assist workshop organizers with the OpenReview setup of this track in addition to others that the workshop may host, we will provide a venue configuration template that supports this feature. Because ICLR tiny and short papers are a participatory initiative, AI-generated papers are not allowed for these formats. AI assistance is permitted, but submissions must be primarily human-authored, reflecting original thought and analysis. See guidance from NYU and MIT on the distinction between AI-generated and AI-assisted work. See this page for a history of the ICLR tiny papers initiative. Participation Limits Each individual may be listed as an organizer on no more than two submitted workshop proposals, and must disclose any other workshop proposals they are involved in organizing. Each individual may be listed as a speaker or panelist in no more than two distinct workshop proposals. Each workshop proposal may include a maximum of eight organizers. Each role, whether an advisory role or a student volunteer role, counts toward the limit of eight organizers. Reviewer nomination As a new requirement this year, we ask each workshop to nominate one or more mid-career or senior researchers who are not among the workshop organizers to serve on the workshop proposal review committee. This will help us accommodate the growing number of submissions and encourage workshops to contribute back to the broader ICLR workshop community. Managing Chair and Reviewer Conflicts of Interest Workshop chairs cannot be organizers nor give invited talks at any workshop, but can submit papers and give contributed talks. Workshop reviewers cannot review any proposal on which they are listed as an organizer or invited speaker, and may not accept invitations to speak at any workshop they have reviewed after the workshop is accepted. Workshop chairs and reviewers cannot review or shape acceptance decisions about workshops with organizers from within their organization. (For large corporations, this means anyone in the corporation world-wide). Managing Organizer Conflicts of Interest Workshop organizers cannot give talks at the workshops they organize. They can give a brief introduction to the workshop and/or act as a panel moderator. Workshop organizers should state in their proposal how they will manage conflicts of interest in assessing submitted contributions. At a minimum, an organizer should not be involved in the assessment of a submission from someone within the same organization. Plan Well for In-Person Workshop organizers should strictly aim for hosting an in-person event. However, we strongly encourage the organizers to account for exceptional circumstances, such as visa issues or other constraints. LLM usage policy Workshop organizers are recommended to follow the Policies on Large Language Model Usage at ICLR 2027 AIPolicyForAuthors , but have the flexibility to establish their own AI usage policies. The only exception is the Tiny Papers track, which does not permit AI-generated content due to requirements associated with its funding. In this iteration of ICLR workshops, the conference will provide tools to flag AI-generated papers, reviews, and meta-reviews. For workshops open to AI serving as primary authors and/or reviewers of workshop papers, please claim the role of AI participation in the workshop proposal. Closer to the workshop date, organizers will be sent a form to confirm they meet the requirements outlined above. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in early rejection of the proposal or, if the proposal has already been accepted, cancellation of the workshop. Final decisions are at the discretion of the ICLR 2027 Workshop Chairs. Other Guidance and Expectations for Workshop Proposals We encourage, and expect, diversity in the organizing team, speakers, and other invited participants. This includes diversity of viewpoint and thinking regarding the topics discussed at the workshop, gender, ethnicity, affiliations, seniority, geographic location, etc. If a workshop is part of a series, organizers are encouraged to include and identify organizers, speakers, and other invited participants who have not organized or participated in previous editions. Organizers should articulate how they have addressed diversity in their proposal in each of these senses Since the goal of the workshop is to generate discussion, sufficient time and structure needs to be included in the program for this. Proposals should explicitly articulate how they will encourage broad discussion. Workshop proposals should list explicitly what the problems are they would like to see solved, or at least advances made, as part of their workshop. They should explain why these are important problems and how the holding of their proposed workshop will contribute to their solution. Workshops should not primarily be a venue for work that has been previously published in other conferences on machine learning, including the ICLR main track. Organizers should make this clear in their calls and explain in their proposal how they will encourage the presentation of ongoing or novel machine learning work. We encourage workshop submissions of varying lengths and scopes, in particular as an avenue for junior and new researchers to start participating in the ICLR community. Organizers should articulate what they hope to achieve from the format proposal beyond the talks listed. With the extraordinary growth of ICLR, and noting the impossibility of accurately predicting attendance and time zone differences, organizers should explain how they will provide access to the content of the workshop for those who cannot attend in person. This might include recording of talks, publishing short working papers or posters on the web, having a follow-up special issue of a journal, curating and maintaining a web page with a range of content, or other ideas. Workshops should allow for choice of attendance based on content. Good workshops will put talk titles up publicly prior to site publication and note the archival status of their submissions. Organizers should articulate how they will do this. Organizing a workshop is a complex task, and proposals should outline the organizational experience and skills of the proposed organizers (as a team). We encourage junior researchers to be involved in workshop organization, but prefer some collective experience in organizing a complex event. Minimum Information Requirements Workshop summary Tentative schedule Invited speakers/panelists Organizers and biographies ​​Anticipated audience size Plan to get an audience for a workshop (advertising, reaching out, etc.) Diversity commitment Virtual access to workshop materials and outcome Previous related workshops Example Successful Proposals Successful proposals of the past year here can be found here: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICLR.cc/2026/Workshop_Proposals#tab-accept Frequently Asked Questions From Past Workshops Workshop Series We neither encourage nor discourage workshops on topics that have appeared before. Membership of an existing sequence of workshops is irrelevant in the assessment of a workshop proposal (it neither helps or hinders). Workshop proposals will be evaluated solely on their merits for this year’s conference. Please indicate if your workshop is part of an ongoing series (ICLR or other conferences). Overlapping Proposals We will not forcibly merge proposals. If multiple strong proposals are submitted on similar topics, we will choose a single proposal to accept. We may then choose to reach out to the organizers of the rejected proposals to ask whether they would like us to share their proposals with the organizers of the accepted workshop. The organizers of the accepted workshop may then optionally initiate a merge. Workshop Modality This year, ICLR will host only in-person workshops. While all arrangements should be focused on the in-person format, organizers should be ready to accommodate situations where an author or speaker is unable to attend due to exceptional circumstances. For example, organizers could display posters on behalf of authors who cannot be present, or allow them to publicize their work through pre-recorded videos on the workshop website.

Update Workshop Schedule with Opening and Closing Times on iclr.cc: 26 March 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE Complete and Finalize Workshop Schedules in the Organizer Portal: 14 April 2027, 11:59 p.m. AoE The mandatory author notification deadline of 26 February 2027 will not be extended. Note that all proposal organizers, speakers and panelists are required to have an OpenReview profile. Please create an OpenReview Profile at least two weeks before the workshop application deadline on 9 October 2026. Selection Criteria Degree to which the proposal is focused on an important and topical problem, and the degree to which it is expected that the community will find the workshop interesting, exciting, and valuable. Intellectual excitement of the topic. Is it likely to break new ground, or reiterate past debates? Diversity and inclusion. (See expectations below under Other Guidance and Expectations for Workshop Proposals. ) Degree to which the proposed program offers an opportunity for discussion. Degree to which the proposal creates opportunities for under-represented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to engage with the community. (See requirements below under Platform for Tiny or Short Papers .) Quality of proposed invited speakers (including expertise, scientific achievements, and presentation ability). Workshop organizers are required to confirm tentative interest from proposed invited speakers and mention this in their proposal. Degree to which the organizers have offered means to engage in the workshop for those unable to physically attend given that the workshops will be in-person. Organizational experience of the team. Other dimensions in the expectations listed below. Points of difference. What makes this workshop enticingly different to the ICLR workshops held previously? Assessment Process The workshop chairs will appoint a number of reviewers who will provide written assessments of the proposals against the criteria listed above. Reviews will be released to authors. Their reports will be considered by the workshop chairs who will jointly decide upon the selected workshops (subject to the notes on COIs listed below). The final decisions will be made by the workshop chairs via consensus and judgment. Note that in contrast to the number of papers accepted at most conferences there is a natural limit to the number of workshops that can be accepted, dictated by the number of available rooms at the conference venue. Workshop Requirements Honor the Global Notification Deadline Prior until 26 February 2027 By submitting a workshop proposal, workshop organizers commit to notifying those who submit contributions (including talks and posters) to their workshop of their acceptance status before 11.59pm, 26 February 2027 (AOE). In addition, the organizers must make the accepted papers publicly visible on OpenReview and import them into iclr.cc by this date. A timeline should be included in the proposal that will allow for this. Platform Contributed Work Ensure that contributed work is well-featured in the program, and is given visibility through presentation slots and poster sessions. Additionally, your workshop program should effectively engage the audience by allowing for interactive components. Platform for Tiny or Short Papers We encourage each workshop to establish a tiny or short paper track to encourage the submission of late-breaking developments that would most benefit from feedback at ICLR, as well to make their workshops more accessible to potential authors outside the ML conference publication circuit. This tiny or short paper track should prioritize less-than-full-conference papers, welcoming submissions that, for example, present an implementation and evaluation of an unpublished but simple idea, a modest but self-contained theoretical result, a follow-up experiment or re-analysis of a previously published paper, or a fresh perspective on an existing publication. To assist workshop organizers with the OpenReview setup of this track in addition to others that the workshop may host, we will provide a venue configuration template that supports this feature. Because ICLR tiny and short papers are a participatory initiative, AI-generated papers are not allowed for these formats. AI assistance is permitted, but submissions must be primarily human-authored, reflecting original thought and analysis. See guidance from NYU and MIT on the distinction between AI-generated and AI-assisted work. See this page for a history of the ICLR tiny papers initiative. Participation Limits Each individual may be listed as an organizer on no more than two submitted workshop proposals, and must disclose any other workshop proposals they are involved in organizing. Each individual may be listed as a speaker or panelist in no more than two distinct workshop proposals. Each workshop proposal may include a maximum of eight organizers. Each role, whether an advisory role or a student volunteer role, counts toward the limit of eight organizers. Reviewer nomination As a new requirement this year, we ask each workshop to nominate one or more mid-career or senior researchers who are not among the workshop organizers to serve on the workshop proposal review committee. This will help us accommodate the growing number of submissions and encourage workshops to contribute back to the broader ICLR workshop community. Managing Chair and Reviewer Conflicts of Interest Workshop chairs cannot be organizers nor give invited talks at any workshop, but can submit papers and give contributed talks. Workshop reviewers cannot review any proposal on which they are listed as an organizer or invited speaker, and may not accept invitations to speak at any workshop they have reviewed after the workshop is accepted. Workshop chairs and reviewers cannot review or shape acceptance decisions about workshops with organizers from within their organization. (For large corporations, this means anyone in the corporation world-wide). Managing Organizer Conflicts of Interest Workshop organizers cannot give talks at the workshops they organize. They can give a brief introduction to the workshop and/or act as a panel moderator. Workshop organizers should state in their proposal how they will manage conflicts of interest in assessing submitted contributions. At a minimum, an organizer should not be involved in the assessment of a submission from someone within the same organization. Plan Well for In-Person Workshop organizers should strictly aim for hosting an in-person event. However, we strongly encourage the organizers to account for exceptional circumstances, such as visa issues or other constraints. LLM usage policy Workshop organizers are recommended to follow the Policies on Large Language Model Usage at ICLR 2027 AIPolicyForAuthors , but have the flexibility to establish their own AI usage policies. The only exception is the Tiny Papers track, which does not permit AI-generated content due to requirements associated with its funding. In this iteration of ICLR workshops, the conference will provide tools to flag AI-generated papers, reviews, and meta-reviews. For workshops open to AI serving as primary authors and/or reviewers of workshop papers, please claim the role of AI participation in the workshop proposal. Closer to the workshop date, organizers will be sent a form to confirm they meet the requirements outlined above. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in early rejection of the proposal or, if the proposal has already been accepted, cancellation of the workshop. Final decisions are at the discretion of the ICLR 2027 Workshop Chairs. Other Guidance and Expectations for Workshop Proposals We encourage, and expect, diversity in the organizing team, speakers, and other invited participants. This includes diversity of viewpoint and thinking regarding the topics discussed at the workshop, gender, ethnicity, affiliations, seniority, geographic location, etc. If a workshop is part of a series, organizers are encouraged to include and identify organizers, speakers, and other invited participants who have not organized or participated in previous editions. Organizers should articulate how they have addressed diversity in their proposal in each of these senses Since the goal of the workshop is to generate discussion, sufficient time and structure needs to be included in the program for this. Proposals should explicitly articulate how they will encourage broad discussion. Workshop proposals should list explicitly what the problems are they would like to see solved, or at least advances made, as part of their workshop. They should explain why these are important problems and how the holding of their proposed workshop will contribute to their solution. Workshops should not primarily be a venue for work that has been previously published in other conferences on machine learning, including the ICLR main track. Organizers should make this clear in their calls and explain in their proposal how they will encourage the presentation of ongoing or novel machine learning work. We encourage workshop submissions of varying lengths and scopes, in particular as an avenue for junior and new researchers to start participating in the ICLR community. Organizers should articulate what they hope to achieve from the format proposal beyond the talks listed. With the extraordinary growth of ICLR, and noting the impossibility of accurately predicting attendance and time zone differences, organizers should explain how they will provide access to the content of the workshop for those who cannot attend in person. This might include recording of talks, publishing short working papers or posters on the web, having a follow-up special issue of a journal, curating and maintaining a web page with a range of content, or other ideas. Workshops should allow for choice of attendance based on content. Good workshops will put talk titles up publicly prior to site publication and note the archival status of their submissions. Organizers should articulate how they will do this. Organizing a workshop is a complex task, and proposals should outline the organizational experience and skills of the proposed organizers (as a team). We encourage junior researchers to be involved in workshop organization, but prefer some collective experience in organizing a complex event. Minimum Information Requirements Workshop summary Tentative schedule Invited speakers/panelists Organizers and biographies ​​Anticipated audience size Plan to get an audience for a workshop (advertising, reaching out, etc.) Diversity commitment Virtual access to workshop materials and outcome Previous related workshops Example Successful Proposals Successful proposals of the past year here can be found here: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICLR.cc/2026/Workshop_Proposals#tab-accept Frequently Asked Questions From Past Workshops Workshop Series We neither encourage nor discourage workshops on topics that have appeared before. Membership of an existing sequence of workshops is irrelevant in the assessment of a workshop proposal (it neither helps or hinders). Workshop proposals will be evaluated solely on their merits for this year’s conference. Please indicate if your workshop is part of an ongoing series (ICLR or other conferences). Overlapping Proposals We will not forcibly merge proposals. If multiple strong proposals are submitted on similar topics, we will choose a single proposal to accept. We may then choose to reach out to the organizers of the rejected proposals to ask whether they would like us to share their proposals with the organizers of the accepted workshop. The organizers of the accepted workshop may then optionally initiate a merge. Workshop Modality This year, ICLR will host only in-person workshops. While all arrangements should be focused on the in-person format, organizers should be ready to accommodate situations where an author or speaker is unable to attend due to exceptional circumstances. For example, organizers could display posters on behalf of authors who cannot be present, or allow them to publicize their work through pre-recorded videos on the workshop website.

items.content: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI tools and reinforcing AI literacy Fostering international cooperation At international level, the AI Office contributes to a strategic, coherent, and effective EU approach, by: Promoting the EU’s approach to trustworthy AI , including collaboration with similar institutions worldwide Fostering international cooperation and governance on AI, contributing to a global approach to AI Supporting the development and implementation of international agreements on AI Cooperation with institutions, experts and stakeholders The AI Office collaborates with Member States and the wider expert community through dedicated platforms: The European Artificial Intelligence Board (AI Board) is a key advisory body supported by the AI Office that includes representatives from each EU Member States and the European Centre for Algorithmic Transparency (ECAT). The AI Board’s primary role is to ensure the effective implementation of the AI Act across the EU by coordinating national authorities, sharing technical and regulatory expertise and providing advice on AI policy, innovation, and international partnerships. The Scientific Panel of independent experts ensures a strong link with the scientific community. Further technical expertise is gathered in an Advisory Forum , representing a balanced selection of stakeholders, including industry, startups and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), academia, think tanks and civil society. The AI Office also oversees the AI Pact , which allows businesses to engage with the Commission and other stakeholders to share best practices and join activities. This engagement has started before the AI Act entered into force and allows businesses to plan ahead and prepare for the full implementation of the AI Act. To stay up to date and register, check the AI Pact events . The Apply AI Alliance is the main coordination forum bringing together AI providers, industry leaders, academia and the public sector to ensure policy actions are grounded in the real-world needs. Closely connected to the Alliance, an AI Observatory will track AI trends and assess impact of AI in specific sectors. Initiatives promoting the development and adoption of AI The AI Office actively supports innovators through policies and initiatives that spur growth across the EU: The AI Continent action plan , launched in April 2025, explains how to harness the untapped potential of EU researchers and industries, turning EU strengths – such as unparalleled talent and strong traditional industries – into AI accelerators. The plan promotes economic growth and competitiveness in areas such as healthcare, cars, science. The Apply AI Strategy , launched in October 2025, complements the action plan. It aims to boost AI adoption and innovation across Europe, particularly among SMEs. It is designed to enhance the competitiveness of strategic sectors and strengthen the EU’s tech sovereignty. In June 2026, the 'AI omnibus' (part of the Digital Simplification Package ) was adopted, introducing targeted amendments to the AI Act to ensure the rules remain clear, simple, and innovation-friendly. The amendments entered into force on 27 July. The ‘ GenAI4EU ' initiative, part of the 2024 AI innovation package , contributes to the development of novel use cases and emerging applications in 14 industrial sectors and the public sector. Other initiatives aimed at boosting the development and uptake of AI are: AI Factories Testing and Experimentation Facilities (TEFS) and sandboxes European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) AI skills and literacy Job opportunities and collaboration The AI Office recruits talent from a wide range of backgrounds for policy, technical and legal roles and administrative support. To apply, complete the Expression of Interest Form . For inquiries, please contact us at the following addresses: Recruitment: CNECT-AIOFFICE-RECRUITMENT@ec.europa.eu General Inquiries: CNECT-AIOFFICE@ec.europa.eu Important: These email addresses are for inquiries only. Applications must be submitted through the dedicated form, not via email. Quick Links Any question on the AI Act? items.content: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative. On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code. We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement. Our rationale is outlined below. The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources. Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification. We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. American schools. 09 The Trump Administration Rollins released new dietary guidelines that prioritize whole, nutrient-dense foods over processed junk. items.content: NVIDIA Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director November 23, 2026 NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it. The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries. Media Contacts Global contacts for media inquiries. items.content: Data Science Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension Learn how to install Sirius, run supported DuckDB SQL queries on NVIDIA GPUs, and compare analytical query performance and compute costs. Nov 23, 2026 By Allison Ding , Rodrigo Aramburu and Xiangyao Yu Like Discuss (1) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary Sirius is a GPU-native SQL engine released as a DuckDB core extension through collaboration between NVIDIA and DuckLabs. Two SQL commands, INSTALL sirius and LOAD sirius, enable GPU acceleration for supported analytical queries without rewriting SQL or changing schemas. DuckDB handles parsing and optimization while Sirius executes supported query plans on NVIDIA GPUs, with unsupported features falling back to the CPU engine. Benchmark tests using TPC-H queries at scale factors up to 10 TB showed 3.25x to 5.50x speedups and up to 79% lower query-time compute cost with tuned two-GPU configurations. Next Steps Install the Sirius core extension to begin accelerating analytical queries. Explore examples in the Sirius GitHub repository for additional guidance. Join the Sirius Slack community to share results and feedback. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more As datasets grow, analytical queries can take longer to run, slowing down data exploration, pipelines, and applications. For developers using DuckDB, reducing query times helps keep analytics responsive and can lower compute costs. NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release Sirius as a DuckDB core extension, bringing GPU acceleration to DuckDB’s analytical query engine. With two SQL commands, you can install and load Sirius to accelerate supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without rewriting your SQL or changing database schemas. Sirius, developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine. This post introduces the core extension, shows you how to run your first GPU query, and explains how Sirius integrates with DuckDB. Accelerate DuckDB queries without rewriting SQL Sirius accelerates supported queries as a whole. DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU. The core extension brings this capability into DuckDB’s standard workflow: install Sirius, load it, and run your queries. With this release, you can: Install directly from DuckDB. Use INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius; to download and activate the extension. Retain familiar SQL. Execute supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without translating them into a separate GPU programming API. Use CPU fallback. Queries with unsupported features fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine. Start with a small example, then apply the same workflow to your own analytical queries. Run your first GPU query You’ll need DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver. Create a sample dataset Open DuckDB with a file-backed database. duckdb getting_started.duckdb Use DuckDB’s TPC-H extension to generate a small analytical dataset for this example. INSTALL tpch; LOAD tpch; CALL dbgen(sf=0.01); CHECKPOINT; The TPC-H extension creates the example tables, including lineitem , which contains order line items. It supplies sample data for this walkthrough and is separate from the Sirius extension. The CHECKPOINT statement persists the generated data so Sirius can read the native DuckDB tables. Install and load Sirius In the same DuckDB session, install and load Sirius. -- Sirius is approximately 700 MB; download time depends on your connection. INSTALL sirius; LOAD sirius; The core extension automatically selects the CUDA backend for your driver. INSTALL downloads the extension, and LOAD activates it in the current connection. Run an analytical query With Sirius loaded, run the following SQL query. SELECT l_returnflag, SUM(l_quantity) AS total_quantity FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_returnflag ORDER BY l_returnflag; This query groups line items by return flag and calculates the total quantity for each group. Supported queries execute on the GPU while retaining the same SQL syntax used with DuckDB. The query returns: l_returnflag total_quantity A 380456.00 N 774222.00 R 381449.00 You now have a complete workflow: create data, load the extension, and execute an analytical query. The small dataset keeps setup quick and illustrates how to use Sirius; it is not intended to demonstrate a performance advantage. Use the same approach with your own DuckDB tables or supported Parquet workflows. Queries with unsupported features automatically fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine. Understand how Sirius executes queries Sirius integrates GPU execution into DuckDB’s query-processing workflow. DuckDB remains the application’s SQL interface and handles query parsing and optimization. Sirius executes supported queries on the GPU and returns results through the same connection. Figure 1. Query flow through DuckDB and Sirius, including CPU fallback for unsupported queries This integration lets developers continue expressing analytical operations in SQL while using GPU parallelism for supported workloads. The application receives query results through DuckDB, preserving the interface used by existing scripts and applications. Compare Sirius GPU and DuckDB CPU benchmark results We evaluated Sirius against CPU-based DuckDB using cold runs of queries derived from the TPC-H benchmark, with data stored in Amazon S3. Tests covered scale factors 100 (100 GB), 1,000 (1 TB), 3,000 (3 TB), and 10,000 (10 TB), measuring total query runtime and query-time compute cost under default and tuned settings. These tests used pinned development builds. Sirius timings exclude result fetch/export, while DuckDB timings include CSV output. Query-time compute costs cover measured instance runtime and exclude startup, validation, storage, S3, and idle time. Figure 2. Cold-run TPC-H query runtime and compute cost for Sirius and CPU-based DuckDB at SF100, SF1K, SF3K, and SF10K With tuned settings, Sirius running on AWS instances with two NVIDIA GPUs delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations. At SF1K, total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds. At SF3K, runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, delivering a 4.69x speedup. Query-time compute cost at SF3K also decreased by approximately 71%. The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K. The tuned two-GPU configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds compared with 2,369.4 seconds for the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configuration. This represents a 3.25x speedup and approximately 79% lower query-time compute cost . The results also show how workload size affects configuration choices. At SF100, one GPU offered the lowest cost, while two GPUs delivered the shortest runtime. At SF10K, the tuned two-GPU configuration outperformed the tuned single-GPU configuration in both runtime and cost. Tuning was particularly important at this scale: at SF10K, the default configuration with two GPUs was marked “did not finish,” while the tuned configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds. The Sirius repository provides a benchmark runner , query definitions , configuration details , and setup instructions for reviewing the test setup and evaluating performance on your own hardware. Results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions. Get started with Sirius The Sirius core extension brings GPU-accelerated analytics into DuckDB’s familiar SQL workflow. Install the extension, run the example, and explore how GPU execution applies to your data. Install the Sirius core extension. Explore examples in the Sirius GitHub repository. Read the DuckDB release announcement. Read about Sirius performance on ClickBench. Join the Sirius Slack community. As your data grows, use Sirius to accelerate supported queries while keeping your SQL, tools, and workflow in DuckDB. Share your results and feedback with the Sirius community. She educates developers on how NVIDIA APIs, libraries, and tools apply to real-world problems. She holds a master’s degree in applied statistics from Cornell University and a master’s degree in computer science from San Francisco Bay University. View all posts by Allison Ding About Rodrigo Aramburu Rodrigo Aramburu leads developer relations for accelerated data processing at NVIDIA, helping developers adopt and innovate with GPU-accelerated analytics. Previously, he co-founded BlazingSQL and Voltron Data, contributing to the NVIDIA RAPIDS ecosystem and advancing Arrow-native data systems. View all posts by Rodrigo Aramburu About Xiangyao Yu Xiangyao Yu is an assistant professor of computer sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, specializing in database systems. His research focuses on GPU-accelerated databases, cloud-native databases, and high-performance SQL analytics and transaction processing. Before joining UW–Madison, he completed a postdoctoral appointment and a Ph.D. at MIT. Xiangyao is a recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, the Sloan Research Fellowship, and the VLDB Early Career Research Contribution Award. View all posts by Xiangyao Yu Comments

items.content: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 49 +43 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate job

If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape.
